seoDescription: Discover how Pydantic supercharges Python applications by enforcing data integrity. This guide explores how to move beyond Python's dynamic typing with Pydantic's robust data validation and serialization. Learn to define data models using `BaseModel`, leverage built-in types like `EmailStr`, and create custom validators with `@field_validator` and `@model_validator`. See practical examples of serialization control and how Pydantic integrates seamlessly with frameworks like FastAPI to build secure and robust APIs.

chapters.title: Why Python Needs Pydantic
chapters.description: Learn about the problems caused by Python's dynamic typing and how Pydantic provides a solution with robust data validation.

chapters.title: Use Cases and Comparison to Data Classes
chapters.description: Explore key use cases for Pydantic, like API development, and understand how it differs from Python's built-in data classes.

chapters.title: Defining a Basic Pydantic Model
chapters.description: This chapter walks through the project setup and how to define a `User` model inheriting from `BaseModel` using `Enums`, `Field` options, and special types.

chapters.title: Basic Data Validation in Action
chapters.description: See how to use `model_validate` to check data against a Pydantic model and inspect the detailed validation errors it generates.

chapters.title: Implementing Custom Field Validators
chapters.description: Learn to create custom validation logic using the `@field_validator` decorator, regular expressions, and the `mode` parameter for advanced control.

chapters.title: Using Model Validators for Cross-Field Logic
chapters.description: This chapter covers the `@model_validator`, which allows for validating the entire data model at once for complex checks involving multiple fields.

chapters.title: Controlling Data Serialization
chapters.description: Explore Pydantic's serialization features, using `field_serializer`, `model_serializer`, and `model_dump` to customize how objects are converted to other formats.

chapters.title: Integrating Pydantic with FastAPI
chapters.description: Demonstrates the seamless integration between Pydantic and FastAPI, showing how FastAPI automatically validates request bodies against Pydantic models.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.description: A final summary of Pydantic's power for data validation and serialization in real-world Python applications.

summary:
## Why Pydantic?

Python's dynamic typing can lead to unexpected runtime errors when handling data. Pydantic solves this by enforcing **data validation** and **serialization** using Python type hints.

- **Key Principle**: Adopts the **fail-fast** principle, ensuring that data structure and type errors are caught as early as possible.
- **Primary Use Cases**: Indispensable when working with external data sources, such as user input, configuration files, or, most notably, web **APIs**.

## Defining Data Models

Data structures in Pydantic are defined by creating classes that inherit from `pydantic.BaseModel`.

- Fields are declared as class attributes using standard **type annotations** (e.g., `name: str`).
- The `Field` function can be used to provide additional metadata and constraints, such as `description`, `examples`, or default values.
- Pydantic offers specialized types for common validation scenarios:
    - `EmailStr`: Ensures a string is a valid email address.
    - `SecretStr`: Obfuscates the field's value when the model is printed, displaying `**********` instead of the actual secret.
- Standard Python `Enum` types can be used directly as field types for validation.

## Validation Techniques

Pydantic provides a layered approach to data validation.

> [!NOTE]
> Upon instantiation, Pydantic automatically validates input data against the defined field types, raising a `ValidationError` if the data is invalid.

### Custom Field Validation
- Use the `@field_validator("field_name")` decorator to add custom logic for a single field.
- Validator functions must accept the field's value and **must return** a value (either the original or a modified one).
- Use `mode="before"` to run the custom validator *before* Pydantic's internal type validation, allowing for data coercion.
- Use `mode="after"` (the default) to run *after* initial validation.

### Custom Model Validation
- Use the `@model_validator()` decorator for validation logic that requires access to **multiple fields**.
- This is ideal for checks like confirming a password doesn't contain the username.
- The validator method receives the entire model's data as a dictionary and **must return** the (potentially modified) dictionary.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A `@field_validator` must return the validated value, and a `@model_validator` must return the data dictionary. Forgetting to return the value will result in `None` being stored for that field or an error.

## Data Serialization

Serialization is the process of converting a Pydantic model instance into another format, typically a dictionary or JSON.

- **`model_dump()`**: Serializes the instance to a Python dictionary.
- **`model_dump_json()`**: Serializes the instance to a JSON formatted string.
- Control serialization behavior:
    - **Excluding Fields**: Use `Field(exclude=True)` in the model definition to prevent a field from ever being included in serialized output. This is critical for sensitive data like passwords.
    - **Custom Serializers**: Use the `@field_serializer("field_name")` decorator to define custom serialization logic for a specific field, such as converting an `Enum` member to its string name for JSON compatibility.

## Integration with FastAPI

Pydantic is a cornerstone of the **FastAPI** framework, enabling robust and auto-documented APIs.

- When a Pydantic model is used as a type hint for an endpoint's request body, FastAPI automatically:
    1. Parses the incoming JSON from the request.
    2. **Validates** the data against the Pydantic model.
    3. Passes the validated data as a Pydantic model instance to your endpoint logic.
    4. Generates rich, interactive API documentation (e.g., Swagger UI) from the model schema.

> [!TIP]
> You can add an inner `class ConfigDict` to your model to control its behavior. For example, `extra="forbid"` will cause validation to fail if a client sends extra, undefined fields in an API request.
transcription:
## Why Python Needs Pydantic

Python's Dynamic type system is incredibly user-friendly but it can sometimes lead to issues when handling data since we might end up with unexpected results. That's where Pydantic comes in. It's the ideal tool to help us be meticulous when dealing with our data. It's particularly useful when working with external data sources such as APIs or user input.

If you'd like to learn how to design software from scratch, I have a free guide for you. You can get it at ardan.dev/design. The guide covers the seven steps that I follow when designing a new piece of software. Hope it proves helpful in avoiding some of the mistakes that I made in the past. You can also find the link to the guide in the description of this video.

Now, let's dive into Pydantic. Here's the example that I'm going to be working on today. As you can see, it imports a couple of things from Pydantic. So what is Pydantic? It's a library that allows you to do data validation and serialization that relies on the type annotation mechanism in Python. Knowing that your data is valid and it follows certain rules and structures is really helpful, and the earlier you detect this, the better. It's sort of the fail-fast principle that you apply here.

## Use Cases and Comparison to Data Classes

So when you work with data that's not well-structured or defined in the way that you want it to, then it's a good thing to fail fast and fail early on so that data doesn't, I don't know, mess up the rest of your data pipeline. And this is where Pydantic can be really helpful. 

Another area where validation and serialization is really, really useful is in developing APIs. When users send requests to your API, you need to make sure that the data they're providing is valid so that you can't get hacked or anything like that. And this is why Pydantic is also really helpful and that's why it's been widely used by popular frameworks such as FastAPI for data validation.

Pydantic works in a very similar way to data classes. So you use type annotations to indicate the type of instance variables part of an object. The main difference is that Pydantic adds much more powerful validation and serialization options than the built-in data classes. If you don't need those things, then using data classes is perfectly fine, but if you do need validation, then Pydantic is really a great option.

## Defining a Basic Pydantic Model

In the example that I have today, I have a pip project file that contains the dependencies. And as you can see, Pydantic is in there, and on top of that, I've also added an extra which is 'email'. This allows me to do email address validation, and next to that, we also have FastAPI and HTTPX which I'll use in an example later on in the video.

So in this particular example, I have a couple of enums and classes. So there's the `Role` enum which is an `int`, and that's either author, editor, developer, or admin, which can be either one of these three. And then I have a `User` class and that inherits from `BaseModel`. So `BaseModel` is a class that comes from Pydantic and that's basically implements the basics of the whole validation system of Pydantic. And when you define your model, your Pydantic class, you inherit from `BaseModel` and then you add the fields that are supposed to be part of it. So one of them is name.

What Pydantic specifically does is use a combination of these type annotations that you see here and the `Field` function. So in this case, the user has a name, email, password, and a role. And the `Field` function has a couple of options. So one thing that you can do is that you can add some examples of what are valid values for this thing. So here is an example of a name is 'Ariel' or in the case of an email, you can provide examples of a valid email address. You can also provide a description of what it is, and this can then be used by FastAPI for documentation, which is really cool.

So you see that there is another type here called `EmailString`. And this is also something that I imported from Pydantic. So next to these built-in types like strings or integers or anything else that you would like to use, you can also use these types which already have some basic validation for you. So this `EmailString` is a string that's supposed to be an email address, and if you supply something that isn't an email address, this is going to complain. Another example here is password which is a `SecretString`, and that simply means that if you're going to print the password, it's going to print out a bunch of asterisks instead of the actual password. And finally, you can also directly use enums like the `Role` that I defined here and also supply that as a Pydantic type, and then it's also going to make sure that the values that you provide when you create this role actually match the values in this enumerated type. And there's other options as well, for example, `frozen` that allows you to only set it and not change it afterwards. So these are just some examples of how Pydantic can help you get more control over what your data looks like.

## Basic Data Validation in Action

And then what I've done here is define a `validate` function that calls `model_validate` on the user. So this allows us to validate whether data adheres to the user structure, and if so, then I simply print the user, and if not, I print that the user is invalid and I print out the errors. And then in the `main` function, I have a good data example which simply has a name, email, and password. And I have bad data, which has something that's not an email address, and the name is also missing.

When I run this, then this is actually what you get. So the first error that we get is that there is something missing, namely the name. And the second error is a value error, which is in the email field, which is that 'value is not a valid email address.' So this is all already built into Pydantic, so you don't have to write this validation code yourself. Finally, another thing that's nice is that actually you get a reference to the documentation with your error, so you can click on this and look up what the actual error is.

## Implementing Custom Field Validators

But what if you want to do a bit more than just use these built-in types that are offered by Pydantic? Well, you can also write your own custom validators and add them to the classes. So that's what I did here. So I just created a few regexes to validate names and passwords, and then I modified the user `BaseModel` and added these field validators.

So if you want to add a custom validation to a field in a Pydantic object, you use the `field_validator` decorator and you supply the name of the field. So this is typically what that looks like. So you have your `field_validator`, you define a class method, in this case, I'm calling this `validate_name`, makes sense, right? That gets the value and that also should return the value, so you can actually modify it if you want to. In this case, the only thing we're doing is we simply check that this regex actually matches the value that we get, and if not, we raise a `ValueError` that a name should only contain letters and be at least two characters long.

The standard way to build these validation functions is that they should normally either return the value, which is what happens here, or they raise a `ValueError` or an `AssertionError`. You also have some control over when this validation takes place. You can indicate a `mode`; can be 'before' or 'after'. If you choose 'before', it means that the value has not yet been set in the object, and that's what you see here. So I've added a field validator for the role as 'before'. The nice thing about using the 'before' mode is that you can specify what kind of input you want to work with. So in this case, this can be an integer, a string, or an `Role` enum value, and then I simply try to convert the value into the actual `Role` type, and if that doesn't work, I raise a `ValueError`.

If you use the 'before' mode, then these validation functions should be class methods like I defined them here. If instead of the 'before' mode you use the 'after' mode, so that means that the instance is already created, then these are not class methods but these are regular instance methods. So you just pass the `self` and then you can work with the `self` object. And of course you can combine these; you can have both validators for 'before' and for 'after' for certain fields. So you can make this as complicated as you want.

## Using Model Validators for Cross-Field Logic

Next to field validators which validate specific fields in a model, we also have a model validator, which allows you to validate the entire instance data all at once. And that can sometimes be helpful. For example, let's say you want to make sure that a password doesn't contain the username. Well, in this case, if we create a field validator for the password, we don't have access to the username, so we can't do that. But in a model validator, you can because you get all the data in a dictionary in this case. So here you can add some checks like, does it have either name or password? They should be required.

You can add a check that the password doesn't contain the name, which isn't very secure, and you can add other if statements and checks here as well. Now this one, for example, is a password regex check. So I think this one could actually be a separate password validator. But by using a combination of field validators and model validators, you can do your data validation in the way that you see fit. And here you also see a usage of returning the value when you're done validating. So in this case, we hash the password before actually storing it in the instance.

And then finally, I have my `validate` function again. I created some test data. So we have good data, we have data with a bad role, so there is no 'programmer' type, then more bad data, a missing role, or there is a name that's not... that contains invalid characters. We have a duplicate, some missing data, and then basically when we run this, then this is what we get. So for all these things, we get the appropriate validation errors.

## Controlling Data Serialization

By the way, if you're interested in joining a community of developers, I have a free Discord server you can join via the link below. There's tons of very knowledgeable people there. We always have fun discussions about Python and software development in general, so I hope you join.

I mentioned Pydantic also allows you to serialize objects and also has all sorts of settings for that. So here's another example that shows how serialization works. So serialization means that we transform an object, an instance, to some other data format. Often this is JSON data. So here I have again my user class, but what I did in this case, that for the password I added an extra option here, which is `exclude`, and that means that when you serialize this object, that password is not included. We don't want to print the password or include it in the serialized form of the user. So if I scroll down, you see some examples of what you can do to have control over how objects are being serialized. So you can add a `field_serializer` for the role, for example, in case of JSON. So what we want to do in this case is that when we serialize the object, we want to make sure that the name of the role is returned so that we can store that in JSON data.

And similarly, we can have a `model_serializer` that gives us some control over how users are being serialized. And then again, I have the main function with some data and then I can use various modes of serialization. So here I'm serializing to a dictionary using `model_dump` and here I'm serializing to a JSON string. And when it serializes to JSON, then it's actually going to use these field and model serializers since I've indicated that right here as an option. Finally, you can also indicate whether, for example, some things need to be excluded such as the role in this case. So when I run this example, then you see here we have the dict serializer, so that simply returns the role as an actual enum value. The JSON string turns this into a string value. The JSON string without the role simply removes the role. And here finally is an example of serialize that simply encodes all the values to a dictionary. In that case, you see when it prints the password, it actually doesn't print the actual password but uses the secret string print methods.

## Integrating Pydantic with FastAPI

Final thing I want to show you, I mentioned that Pydantic is used by many popular frameworks including FastAPI and that allows you to specify how data should be validated in your REST API when you're using FastAPI. So here's an example of what that looks like. So again, I have my Pydantic user model, and you can specify extra options here that are more suitable to using Pydantic with APIs. So one thing that I've added here, for example, is a configuration setting that forbids adding extra attributes. So you don't want somebody to call your API and just add a bunch of attributes to the body, right? You only want the attributes that are actually being part of the object. So those are the types of settings that you can add here.

Again, we have name, email, and these things work just like before, but now they're part of an API. And I've added a couple of things here as well. So you can add a list of friends, you can have an optional datetime, uh, you can have an ID which is useful if you want to store the user in a database, and you can also define your serializers here so that you specify how, when you return this object in your API, what should happen when you serialize it to JSON. So then in FastAPI, we define the endpoint. So we have getting the users, creating a user, and what's nice is that because we pass the user here as an argument, FastAPI will make sure to actually validate it. And then I have a main function with a test client so that I can just run some tests on using the FastAPI app. And when I run this, then you see it passes all these asserts. So I've just included this in the main file. Normally, you would of course move this out of the main file into a separate test folder so that you can run these things as unit tests. But the important thing is that FastAPI natively integrates really well with Pydantic and that allows you to do lots of validation work and make your API really robust.

## Conclusion

So to conclude, Pydantic is a really powerful library for validating your data, for serializing your data. So if you're building out an API, if you're processing data, then Pydantic is really useful to have in your toolkit.

So I'd like to hear from you. Have you used Pydantic in your project? In what way are you using it and what were your experiences with it? Let me know in the comments. So like I've shown here, Pydantic works really well with FastAPI. If you want to learn more about how FastAPI works, check out this video next where I dive into the details. Thanks for watching and see you next time.
